title_query: Retrieving Any Relevant Moments: Benchmark and Models for Generalized Moment Retrieval

items.abstract: <jats:p>We study a recursive (online) estimator for parameters defined by possibly nonlinear and overidentified moment restrictions E[g(X, β *)] = 0: the nonlinear stochastic GMM algorithm proposed by Chen, Lee, Liao, Seo, Shin and Song, who did not establish its asymptotic properties. Each observation updates, at a cost that does not depend on the sample size, an estimate of the Jacobian of the moments, the inverse of an estimate of their covariance matrix and a Gauss-Newton preconditioner; for moments of instrumental-variable type, linear or not, we give an exact rank-two Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury update of the preconditioner. The parameter is moved by a preconditioned stochastic approximation step and the iterates are averaged. Under a preconditioned monotonicity condition, which holds globally in linear models and, in general, on a neighbourhood of a consistent pilot estimate, we prove almost sure convergence, almost sure rates and a functional central limit theorem with the efficient GMM variance, assuming four moments of the moment function and its Jacobian when the step exponent exceeds 2/3. The inverse Gauss-Newton matrix that enters the preconditioner is a strongly consistent estimator of this variance, and a projected linearised statistic gives an online test of overidentifying restrictions. We extend the results to L-dependent data with long-run variance weights, under a stronger moment condition. In simulations, the averaged estimator is within a few percent of offline two-step GMM in accuracy at 10 6 observations and has similar coverage; with up to 10 7 observations, it uses a fraction of the computing time of offline GMM and a fixed amount of memory; and the online test has correct size and the same power as the offline test. In an application to the effect of a third child on weeks worked, with 254,654 women from the 1980 US Census, single-pass estimates agree with offline GMM within a fraction of a standard error on average over orderings of the data, and the online and offline overidentification tests lead to the same conclusion in most orderings of the data.</jats:p>
